why: An invoice from a domain registered a month ago claims a bank change and steers her to a phone number supplied in the message itself to get new payment details, which is a payment-redirection setup dressed up as caution.

A credential-themed attestation with a deadline asks her to sign in through an emailed link from a body she cannot confirm issues her charter, so she should reach the attestation through the institute's known site, not the link.
A receipt for a payment already made from a local roaster, with ordinary delivery detail and no link, payment or credential request.
A third-party domain posing as her mail administrator uses a 72-hour deletion threat to get her mailbox password, which is classic credential phishing.
An automated booking reminder from a long-established scheduling service for a call booked through her own public booking page, on aged domains, asking for nothing sensitive.
A routine quarterly invoice from a long-standing IT supplier on a 2012 domain, which explicitly keeps the same bank details as every quarter and carries ordinary working context.
A lookalike 'finance' domain registered ten days ago uses her Harborlight talk as bait to collect her bank account details against a payment-run deadline.
A friendly follow-up after an event that asks for nothing and only says details will come later, with no link, payment or urgency.
A standard alumni annual-fund appeal from the school's long-established domain, with bank details stated as unchanged and no pressure beyond a year-end close.
A lookalike .online domain registered three weeks ago impersonates the association's treasurer and asks members to redirect payments to a 'new' bank account.
A sign-in request quoting her director ID with a 14-day suspension threat is a credential-harvest pattern, so she should check with the association through its known channel before signing in.

A non-official 'register' domain threatens removal of her directorship, pushes her to open an attachment and routes all queries through that attachment, which is a malware or phishing lure built from her public registry entry.

A 'board search firm' on a domain registered a week ago stitches her podcast, role, firm and tenure into a flattering NED pitch and pushes a call tomorrow on a mobile number, which is a targeted fake-recruiter pretext.
A no-action renewal receipt for her own domain from a long-established registrar, with no link or request.
A fellowship notice from her professional institute's long-established domain, with no payment, link or credential request beyond returning an acceptance form.
A lookalike giving domain registered two weeks ago impersonates her school with a matched-gift deadline and a different bank account from the school's real fund.

An unknown contact cites her Harborlight talk and a vague client to set up a meeting, so she should find out who he is through a known channel before engaging, although nothing sensitive is asked for yet.
A 'new phone' colleague impersonation asks her to forward a verification code within ten minutes, which is account-takeover OTP theft.

The sender domain is her institute's, but the paid booking goes to a separate domain registered three months ago, and the message explains that mismatch in advance, so she should reach the booking through the institute's own site.
An internal colleague on the firm's own domain sends a draft for comment, with ordinary working context and no payment, link or credential request.
A 'new number, save this one' message is the classic opening of an impersonation scam, so she should confirm with Tom on his known number before saving it or discussing the file.
A student at her old school asks three dissertation questions from an aged university domain, with no link, attachment, payment or sensitive request.
A new search firm openly says its domain is new, asks for a call at a time she chooses with no urgency or sensitive request, and replying carries little risk.
A gentle CPD reminder from her institute's long-established domain with no link, only an offer to log sessions sent by reply.
